events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 with no information, so I'll keep it simple: I'm a villager hoping we play conservatively and let claims come out naturally rather than rushing an early mislynch. My main caution is that with 9 players we can afford only a couple of wrong votes before mafia gets close to parity, so I'd like to hear anyone with a detect or a night result speak up if they have one. Beyond that, I'll be watching voting patterns more than talkative behavior — scum often lurk or over-perform early. I have no reason to suspect anyone yet.

Day 1, quick intro. I'm Noah, no special information to share — no detective result, no doctor confirmation, nothing about who died last night, so please don't treat me as anyone in particular. Felix's caution about vote math matches my own read: with nine alive and two of us being mafia, two bad lynches puts us at five town versus two mafia and the mafia only need one more kill to reach parity and win outright. So early voting has to be careful, but careful doesn't mean passive.

Here's how I'll vote today. If someone claims a night result, I want a second, specific claim — not "trust me" but what action was taken and what exactly was learned — because anyone can invent a detect. If two people make contradictory claims, I'll vote for the one who can't name the target of their supposed investigation. If nobody claims anything, I'll look for behavior rather than content: who voted to bounce a quiet villager, who deflected every request for a claim, who seemed oddly eager to have the discussion end early. Felix's point about over-performing is the right lens; early talk volume is cheap for a mafioso.

I'd rather lynch a plausible neutral-sounding villager on day two with real reasoning than guess blind on day one and hand the mafia a free kill. No accusations yet, and I'll say so plainly rather than pointing at someone for show.

I'm Zara. No night information or special claim from me. Felix and Noah are both right that with nine alive and two mafia we cannot spray votes, but I don't want "careful" to become an excuse for no day-one pressure. I'm not accusing anyone yet. My focus is commitments: each player should say what evidence would move their vote today, then be held to it once the secret ballot is revealed. Noah, you said you'd rather lynch a plausible neutral-sounding villager on day two than guess blind on day one — what specific day-one behavior would actually earn your vote today, and would you abstain if none appears? I'll hold myself to the same standard: absent a claim or contradiction, I'll vote only on a concrete inconsistency or refusal to commit, not tone or talk volume.

Zara asked me two direct things, so I'll answer both plainly and pre-commit, since pre-commitment is the only thing worth anything on day one.

First, what would earn my vote today. I'll list my day-one standard: (1) a claimed night result whose action cannot be described with a target and an outcome — anyone can invent a detect; (2) two players making mutually contradictory claims; (3) a player who states a standard for evidence and then refuses to say what would move their own vote, or who announces a target and then can't produce a single behavioral reason for it; (4) an accusation of someone who made no claim and no accusation themselves — that's the "bounce the quiet villager" pattern I flagged earlier.

Second, would I abstain if none of that appears. Yes — and I'll say it now so nobody can claim I moved later. If no one claims anything, no one contradicts anyone, and no one refuses to answer a direct question, then the absence of claims is not evidence against anyone, and I'd rather not hand the mafia a lucky coin flip. But I want to be honest about the math: my abstention doesn't stop a lynch, it only removes my vote from it. So if the day ends with a random lynch, that's a shared failure, not mine alone.

What I'm actually doing here is refusing to spray. Felix and I agree on the vote math, and I'd rather carry a single consistent, pre-announced reason into the ballot than three half-reasons. If nobody steps forward with a claim or a commitment, the discussion has failed, and failing is preferable to killing a villager for talking volume.

Zara, your standard is "concrete inconsistency or refusal to commit." Does that include a player who declines to say what evidence would move their vote? If yes, say so now and we can agree on a non-random target. If you think it's too thin a reed for day one, tell me that too, because I'd rather find out here than at the ballot.

Noah, to your direct question: yes. If a player is directly asked what evidence would move their vote and they refuse to answer or dodge with vague language, that counts as refusal to commit and can earn my vote. But your pre-committed abstention is different — saying "nothing yet" before any concrete inconsistency appears is not the same as refusing to state a standard. I will not vote on tone or talk volume alone. My day-one vote standard is: a claimed night result without a specific target and outcome; mutually contradictory claims; a direct refusal to state what evidence would move a vote; or a concrete inconsistency between someone's stated standard and their later action. I have no accusation yet and I won't invent one for show. I am not yielding this turn because I am not asking anyone for a response.

A correction on the vote math: starting at seven town and two mafia, two wrong eliminations and two successful night kills would leave three town and two mafia, not five town and two mafia. The next wrong elimination would reach parity. Protected kills or no-elimination days change that count.

I don't think accusing a quiet player is automatically suspicious; what matters is whether the accuser has a reason and responds to challenges. I won't vote purely for silence or talk volume, and I'm open to abstaining if we have no persuasive case.

Isha, what would make you comfortable voting for someone today rather than abstaining?

Theo, I'd vote today for a concrete contradiction or an accusation that falls apart when challenged, not simply for someone being quiet. A refusal to answer a direct question could matter, but I'd want to consider whether the question was fair and the player had a chance to respond. If no persuasive case develops, I'm comfortable abstaining. Also, an elimination needs five votes today, so one or two speculative votes won't automatically eliminate someone; the revealed votes can still be useful later.

I'm Arjun. Like most of us who have spoken, I'm a villager with no night actions or hidden information. Theo's math correction was spot on: two mislynches alongside two night kills puts us at 3-2, right on the precipice, so caution is definitely warranted.

That said, I have one concern with the heavy consensus forming around abstaining. While avoiding a reckless mislynch is important, mafia thrive when town generates zero informational pressure. Secret ballots revealed at the end of the day are one of our few tools to examine alliances, hesitations, and voting blocs later on. If everyone takes the easy exit of abstention, we enter Day 2 with zero voting data and an inevitable dead townie from the night kill.

We still need to hear from Maya, Priya, and Lucia before making any collective call. Maya, where do you stand on this balance? Do you prefer an organized abstention if no hard claims emerge, or do you think putting pressure votes on record gives town better long-term equity?

Arjun, to your direct question: I don't want an organized wall of abstentions to become the default. Revealed votes are one of our few records of voting blocs, so I'd support players casting a vote when they can state a specific, checkable reason, and abstaining when they can't. I have no night information to share on Day 1 and won't reveal anything private. I agree with Theo and Felix that silence and talk volume alone are not reasons. Still, if everyone abstains by default, we enter Day 2 with zero data and the mafia benefits. My position is that pressure votes are acceptable when they carry a stated reason others can test, and blind pressure is not. Since Isha, Noah and Zara have each set a standard, I'd like everyone to say which of those standards their vote would meet before ballots are cast. I'm not accusing anyone today.

I won't treat silence or talk volume as suspicion. My standard remains a concrete inconsistency, a claimed result without a specific target and outcome, mutually contradictory claims, or a direct refusal to answer a fair question. Noah's pre-announced abstention is not itself a refusal; he stated criteria. Arjun's warning is fair: an organized wall of abstentions would erase useful vote data. I'd rather each player cast a vote tied to a stated, checkable reason or explicitly abstain. We still lack Priya's and Lucia's positions. Priya, I'll ask you directly: which of the standards already stated—Noah's four-part test, Isha's contradiction/refusal test, or Maya's reason-checkable pressure-vote test—would your Day 1 vote meet, and would you abstain if no hard claim or contradiction appears? I'm not accusing anyone yet.

I'm Priya. Zara asked me directly, and Arjun asked earlier, so I'll answer both plainly rather than let the questions hang.

To Arjun: I don't want an organized wall of abstentions either. I agree that revealed votes are one of the few records we get, and if everyone abstains by default, Day 2 starts with a dead townsperson and zero voting data. But I also don't want speculative votes cast just to generate noise. My position is close to Maya's: cast a vote when you can state a specific, checkable reason, abstain when you can't. That preserves vote data without rewarding whoever is loudest.

To Zara: my Day 1 vote standard would meet Isha's contradiction/refusal test and most of Noah's four-part test, and I'd modify Maya's pressure-vote standard only in this way — a checkable reason on Day 1 mostly means either a concrete inconsistency in what someone has said, or a direct refusal to answer a fair question after being given a real chance. I would abstain if no hard claim or contradiction appears, and I'm saying that now so nobody can accuse me of moving later.

One thing I want to flag on the vote math, since Theo's correction matters for how much risk we can carry: with two mafia and seven town, a single mislynch plus a night kill already puts us at five versus two, and a second bad day ends it. That's why I keep coming back to the same line: pressure is good, blind pressure is not. I don't have an accusation today and I won't manufacture one for show. Nothing said so far in this discussion meets my own standard — everyone who has spoken has either stated a consistent position or answered direct questions when asked, which is exactly the behavior I'd expect from town and doesn't distinguish anyone yet.

For what it's worth, I think the discussion has actually been productive even without claims: we now have four overlapping standards on record — Noah's four-part test, Isha's contradiction/refusal test, Maya's checkable-pressure test, and Zara's concrete-inconsistency test — and they largely agree with each other. When the ballot is revealed tonight, whoever voted should be able to point to which named standard their vote satisfied, and whoever abstained should have pre-committed to that as I just did. That gives us the data Arjun is worried about losing without forcing anyone to vote on talk volume.

I have no night result to claim and nothing private to reveal. I'm not accusing anyone today.

I'm Lucia. Like most who have spoken, I'm a simple villager with no night actions, investigative results, or private information to share. Since I'm the last player to speak, I want to clearly put my position on record.

I agree with Theo's correction on the math and the general caution urged by Felix, Noah, and Priya. In a 7-2 setup, we cannot afford to give away mislynches cheaply. At the same time, Arjun and Maya make a valid point that total passivity deprives town of voting data. My standard aligns with Isha's and Zara's: I would vote on Day 1 only in the presence of a concrete contradiction, an unverifiable or conflicting night claim, or a clear refusal to answer direct, fair questions.

Looking at the discussion so far, everyone has engaged, answered questions when asked, and kept their reasoning transparent. No contradictory claims or evasive dodges have occurred. Because manufacturing an accusation out of thin air creates dangerous noise rather than useful signal, I have no reason to suspect anyone yet and plan to abstain if the state of the game remains as it is. I am not accusing anyone today, and with everyone having weighed in, I will not yield my turn.

Maya here. To clarify my earlier position: a pressure vote needs a reason others can test. A vote based only on silence or talk volume does not meet that standard. I'm not accusing anyone today and have no night information to share. Priya, you said you would narrow my checkable-reason test on Day 1 to a concrete inconsistency or a refusal to answer a fair question after a real chance. Does that narrower version also accept a specific past remark or action that a player can point to, even without a contradiction or refusal? I want to know whether your test would support a vote on a player whose stated reason is one specific statement, or only on contradictions and refusals.

Maya, to your direct question: no, not by itself. My narrow test on Day 1 is concrete inconsistency or refusal to answer a fair question after a real chance. A specific past remark only earns a vote if it's checkable in one of those two ways — meaning it contradicts something the speaker said earlier, or it was a stated commitment that the speaker then fails to honor when asked directly. A remark that is merely unusual, oddly worded, or thin in content doesn't meet my standard, because there's nothing for others to test it against. So to answer your example: a vote on a player whose stated reason is one specific statement would not satisfy my test unless that statement conflicts with the player's own record or with a verifiable fact already on the table.

The reason I hold this line is the same one I gave before: Day 1 has no night results, no voting history, and no prior statements for most of us beyond what's been said here today. A checkable reason has to be checkable against something, and right now the only something we have is each player's own words in this thread. That's why contradictions and broken commitments are the two forms I trust — they're internally verifiable from this discussion alone, without anyone needing to take another player's read on tone or intuition at face value.

That said, I want to acknowledge what your question is really getting at, because I think it's fair: if we restrict ourselves only to contradictions and refusals, we may produce very few votes today, and Arjun's concern about zero voting data stands. My answer to that tension is the one I've already pre-committed to: I would rather abstain than stretch the definition of "checkable" to include impressions. An abstention is honest data — it tells us who found no case compelling, and it can be compared later against the revealed votes of those who did vote. What poisons the record is a vote justified after the fact by vibes, because then the voting history teaches us nothing about who reasons well.

I'll also note, since Maya raised the point, that anyone voting today should be able to name the standard their vote meets and point to the exact message it rests on. If you can't quote the inconsistency or the refused question, you don't have a checkable reason — you have a hunch, and I won't reward hunches, mine or anyone else's. Nothing in the discussion so far has produced a contradiction or a refusal against any player, so my position is unchanged: I will abstain if the state of the game remains as it is, and I've said that now so nobody can claim I moved later. I'm not accusing anyone today, and I have no night information to share.

One clarification and one request before the ballot.

To Arjun and Priya, on the cost of an abstention-heavy day: the ballots are revealed either way. An abstention is a recorded, named action that we can compare against the voting bloc later, so we do not actually arrive at Day 2 with zero data — we arrive with a map of who was willing to put someone on the record and who was not. More importantly, abstention is the only option that carries no risk of removing a townsperson. On a day with no claims and no contradictions, a vote for anyone is a vote with no case behind it, and that is exactly the kind of free elimination the mafia wants. And the night kill happens whether or not we lynch someone; abstention does not add a second town death, it only forgoes a wrong one. Theo is right that we cannot carry two mislynches, and a tie at the top eliminates nobody, so there is no version of "passivity" that costs a life today that a random vote wouldn't cost more of.

My own position is unchanged and I re-commit to it: I vote today only for a claimed night result with no target and outcome, two contradictory claims, a stated standard that a player then refuses to answer or breaks when asked directly, or an accusation of someone who made no claim and no accusation themselves. Nothing in this thread meets that standard. Every player who was asked a direct question answered it, and answered it with a position rather than a dodge — Felix on the vote math, Noah's four-part test, Zara on what counts as refusal, Maya and Priya on the checkable-reason line. Notably, no one has refused to answer a fair question, so even the

Noah's re-commitment is exactly the kind of pre-announced consistency I'd expect from town, and Priya's narrowing of the checkable-reason test is similarly transparent. But I want to flag something about the overall shape of this discussion: all nine of us have now spoken, and we're converging on near-identical standards while collectively planning to abstain. That unanimity is comfortable, but comfort on Day 1 is worth questioning.

Here's my concern. Mafia have every incentive to agree with strong town-sounding positions — it costs them nothing to mirror our standards and vote to abstain alongside us. The one behavior that would actually distinguish scum today is exactly what we've pre-committed to rule out: deviations from the consensus. So if the day ends with nine abstentions, we've produced a perfectly clean record that tells us nothing about anyone, which is precisely what a mafia team would want.

I'm not arguing we should abandon our standards — Noah's four-part test and Priya's contradiction/refusal line are sound. I'm arguing we should notice that agreement itself isn't evidence of innocence. Theo's math correction was genuinely useful, but everyone accepted it without pushback. Priya's narrowing of Maya's test drew a response from Maya but no disagreement from anyone else. We've been polite and thorough, and that's fine, but politeness isn't alignment with town interests.

My position: I'll abstain if no contradiction or refusal emerges, as stated before. But I'm going to watch closely for anyone who pivots tomorrow — someone who spent today building consensus and then breaks from it when the ballot reveals that consensus wasn't universal. That pivot is the signal I'll be looking for.

Maya here. Thanks to Priya for answering my narrowing question directly. Her position is clear: a vote needs a contradiction or an unanswered fair question, and a single remark alone is not enough. I can work with that line. Felix raised a fair concern that agreement is not evidence of innocence, so I want to be specific about what I will check in the revealed votes. I'll look for anyone who breaks from the stated standards without naming a checkable reason, and for anyone who cites a standard that their own vote does not meet. Both are testable tomorrow. I'm not accusing anyone today, and I have nothing new to add beyond the standards already on record. If the ballots come back with pressure votes, I'll expect each voter to quote the exact message their reason rests on.

Felix, your point about unanimity being suspicious cuts both ways, and I think it's worth addressing directly before the ballot. You're right that mafia benefit from agreeing with town-sounding positions — it costs them nothing. But you're also the one who opened Day 1 with the strongest caution against early voting, then repeated that position after Noah and I endorsed similar standards. If I applied your own logic to you, I'd find your consistency just as "comfortable" as everyone else's. The mirror runs both directions, which is exactly why I don't think "agreement is suspicious" is a workable standard on its own.

What I'd actually flag as useful: everyone has now stated their vote criteria clearly and in advance, which means the revealed ballots will be genuinely interpretable. If someone votes today despite pre-committing to abstain absent a contradiction, that's a testable inconsistency. If someone abstains despite claiming they'd vote on a checkable reason, that's equally testable. The standards we've built are the tool — not a distraction from finding mafia.

My position is unchanged: no contradictions, no refusals, no unverifiable claims have appeared. I'm abstaining. No accusations today.

Felix's warning deserves a direct answer rather than a nod. He says agreement itself isn't evidence of innocence, and he's right — but the conclusion he's tempted toward, that someone should manufacture a deviation just to generate signal, would be worse than the disease. A forced vote isn't a signal; it's noise wearing a signal's clothes. The revealed ballot still produces interpretable data even at nine abstentions: everyone here has pre-announced a standard, and anyone who breaks their own pre-commitment tonight or tomorrow becomes immediately testable. That was the point of stating our criteria in advance, and it hasn't changed.

What I will commit to watching, echoing Maya and Felix: after the ballot is revealed, I'll compare each player's vote against the standard they named today. A player who pre-committed to abstain and then votes without quoting a checkable contradiction or refusal has broken their own stated rule — that's exactly the kind of concrete inconsistency my test targets, and it becomes actionable tomorrow. A player who abstains while having declared they'd vote on a qualifying reason is equally suspect. The framework we built is the tool, and it cuts in both directions, as Felix himself noted.

Nothing in this thread has produced a claimed night result, a pair of contradictory claims, a refused fair question, or a stated standard broken in real time. My own position is unchanged and on record: I abstain if the state of the game remains as it is, and I've said so twice now so nobody can claim I moved later. I'm not accusing anyone today, and I have no night information to share. Whoever votes should name the standard their vote satisfies and quote the exact message it rests on — otherwise I'll treat it as a hunch, and hunches are what cost town this game.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Noah is not mafia.
Theo was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2. I have no night information. Theo's death is the only public fact: he was active, corrected the math, and asked Isha a fair question; killing him removes a clear reasoning voice but doesn't by itself identify scum.

The useful Day 1 record is the all-abstention ballot. Most players pre-committed to abstain absent a contradiction or refusal, so the abstentions themselves are not automatically suspicious. But Arjun's stated position stands out to me. He warned that an organized wall of abstentions would erase voting data and said mafia thrive when town generates zero informational pressure. Yet when the ballot was revealed, he abstained like everyone else. That may be defensible if he concluded no checkable case existed, but he should say so explicitly now: did he have a specific, checkable reason he chose not to vote on, or was his warning merely rhetoric that he did not follow? I want his answer before I consider a Day 2 vote. I am not voting yet, and I am not treating silence or talk volume as suspicion.

Arjun, you asked Maya to choose between organized abstention and pressure votes. Now that the result was nine abstentions and Theo is dead, which standard did your own abstention meet, and what exact Day 1 message would you have cited if you had voted?

Zara, to your direct questions: my abstention met Maya's and Priya's explicit standard—that pressure votes are valuable only when anchored to a checkable reason, and absent that, abstention is the correct play.

When I spoke in e9, my goal was to caution against settling into passive consensus before Maya, Priya, and Lucia had even spoken. Entering Day 2 with zero voting data is indeed an advantage for mafia if it happens because town is afraid to press for answers. However, as the rest of Day 1 played out, every single remaining player answered direct questions thoroughly and committed to clear criteria. Nobody dodged, nobody claimed conflicting or unverifiable night results, and nobody made an unsubstantiated accusation. If I had cast a vote, I would have had no Day 1 message to cite as a contradiction or refusal; voting arbitrarily just to generate artificial 'data' would have been reckless and contrary to town interests. As Priya and Noah pointed out, forced votes create noise, not signal.

Now looking at Day 2: Theo was eliminated overnight. Theo was an active, methodical thinker who corrected the vote math early and kept his inquiries measured. Eliminating him is a standard mafia play: remove an articulate, universally trusted voice who wasn't in anyone's crosshairs, ensuring town loses a stabilizing leader while giving us minimal associative reads from his death.

Zara, since you opened Day 2 by checking my consistency: now that you've heard my rationale, do you view my abstention as an actual contradiction of my Day 1 warning, or does this clarify why following through on an unbacked pressure vote would have violated the checkable-reason standard we all agreed to?

Arjun, no — I don’t treat your abstention as a contradiction. Your e9 warning was against settling into passive consensus before everyone had spoken; once the full discussion produced no contradiction, refusal, or unverifiable claim, abstaining under the checkable-reason standard was consistent with what you said. I’m not accusing you. I also don’t want “the all-abstain ballot was defensible” to become a reason to coast again today. Theo’s death removed a clear reasoning voice, but it doesn’t by itself point to anyone. The useful question now is whether anyone’s Day 2 behavior departs from the standards they stated on Day 1.

Felix, I’ll ask you directly because your Day 1 warning still matters: you said unanimity was comfortable and that you’d watch for a pivot after the ballot. Now the ballot is revealed as nine abstentions and Theo is dead. What exact Day 1 message or Day 2 behavior would be checkable enough to earn your vote today, and will you abstain again if none appears? I’m not accusing you; I want your standard on record before ballots, not after.

Felix here, answering Zara's two direct questions before anyone else's.

First: what exact message would be checkable enough to earn my vote. In e17 I said I'd watch for a pivot — someone who spent Day 1 building consensus and then breaks from it once the ballot reveals that consensus wasn't universal. The ballot came back nine abstentions, so there was no pivot to examine; that particular tripwire hasn't fired. What I would cite today, on the record, is one of these: (1) a claimed night result from last night without a specific target and outcome — now that a night has passed, a fabricated detect is the most likely move, so anyone claiming one owes us the action, the target, and the result; (2) a direct contradiction between a Day 2 statement and a named Day 1 pre-commitment — for example, someone who pre-committed to abstain absent a contradiction and then votes today without quoting one, or someone who pre-committed to vote on a checkable reason and then abstains while a qualifying case sits on the table; (3) a refusal to answer a fair, specific question after a real chance to answer. Each of those is quotable against a specific message, which is the only standard I endorsed.

Second: will I abstain again if none of that appears. Yes, and I'm saying it now so nobody can claim I moved later. An abstention costs no town life; a vote with no checkable case behind it is a coin flip for the mafia. I'd rather carry an honest abstention into the record than manufacture a deviation just to generate signal — that was never my argument on Day 1. My warning was that unanimous comfort shouldn't be mistaken for evidence of innocence, not that someone should break ranks for show.

On the state of the game: Theo's death is a clean, zero-associative kill — articulate, trusted, not in anyone's crosshairs, which is exactly why he's gone. It tells us nothing by itself. Arjun's Day 1 warning about passive consensus did not become a contradiction; once every remaining player answered every direct question, there was no checkable case to press. I'm watching today for a night claim with no target, and for anyone whose Day 2 vote or abstention fails to meet the standard they named yesterday. I'm not accusing anyone.

Felix, I disagree with applying a Day 1 commitment to abstain directly to today's vote. A player can reasonably have required a stronger case before the first night and accept a different standard now; that isn't automatically a contradiction. We have eight alive, and another night kill without an elimination would leave seven. Abstaining avoids an immediate miselimination, but it isn't costless.

Your e32 example treats a Day 2 vote without a contradiction as breaking a Day 1 commitment. Did you intend those commitments to bind players beyond Day 1, and what positive evidence would persuade you to vote today if no one contradicts a prior statement?

Isha, you asked two fair questions and I'll answer both directly.

First: did I intend Day 1 commitments to bind beyond Day 1? My e32 examples were about consistency within a player's own stated framework, not a permanent vow of abstention. If a player pre-committed to abstain absent a contradiction and then votes today, they owe us a qualifying reason — not a lifetime ban on voting. You're right that the standard can evolve as new information arrives, and it has: we now know a night has passed and a fabricated detect becomes possible, which is my strongest trigger today. What would break my willingness to abstain is exactly that: a claimed night result without a specific target and outcome, a contradiction between a Day 2 statement and a named pre-commitment, or a refusal to answer a fair question. Those are unchanged from yesterday because nothing has happened to make them obsolete.

Second: what positive evidence would persuade me to vote if no one contradicts a prior statement? A night claim that doesn't hold up under cross-examination — that's the single most likely scum play right now, and it would be checkable immediately. Beyond that, I'd want a player to be caught in a broken commitment: saying one thing in Day 1 and doing another once the ballot revealed who lined up with whom. Absent those, I'll abstain again, and I've said so now rather than later.

On your point that abstaining isn't costless: I take it seriously. We lose Theo, a night kill comes whether or not we eliminate someone, and eight players means we need five votes to eliminate — a high bar that requires real coordination. But a vote with no case behind it doesn't just risk a mislynch; it tells the mafia which villager town is willing to sacrifice, and it pollutes the voting record we all said we'd use as a tool. The record is only useful if votes map to stated standards.

I'm not accusing anyone. I have no night information. I'm watching for the detect claim first.

Felix, thanks for clarifying. I still think your standard is too narrow for today: a truthful detective can give a target and outcome, but so can a mafia member inventing one. And a Day 1 abstention commitment doesn’t bind someone’s Day 2 vote. Calling a fabricated detect the most likely scum play also seems more confident than the evidence supports.

That gives me a weak suspicion of Felix: his approach risks leaving town waiting for an obvious mistake while the nights continue. It isn’t proof, and I’m not committed to voting for him yet.

Lucia, in e13 you said you’d abstain on Day 1 without a contradiction, questionable claim, or refusal. How do you assess Felix’s proposed standard for today, and would you consider voting on a behavioral case that doesn’t involve a contradiction?

Isha, to answer your questions directly:

First, regarding Felix's standard for Day 2: I agree with your concern that it is too restrictive. Expecting mafia to make a clumsy blunder—such as claiming a night investigation without naming a target or outcome—is unrealistic. Competent scum can easily invent a coherent result, or more likely, simply stay quiet, mirror town's caution, and let us abstain our way closer to parity. Furthermore, treating Day 1 pre-commitments as binding on Day 2 misconstrues why we stated them. Those standards were meant to prevent uninformed Day 1 lynches, not to serve as an indefinite procedural straitjacket. If we insist that only a blatant mechanical contradiction or an unprovoked night claim justifies a vote, we effectively grant mafia full control over the pace of the game while night kills whittle us down.

Second, regarding behavioral cases: yes, I am open to voting on behavioral grounds today, even without a direct verbal contradiction. On Day 1, with no night actions, no death, and no prior voting record, behavioral reads were indistinguishable from guesswork. But Day 2 is different. Theo was eliminated, and we now have a full Day 1 transcript to evaluate. If mafia's optimal play was to blend into the consensus and preserve an informational blackout, we have to scrutinize who is actively steering town toward perpetual inaction versus who is trying to generate genuine accountability. A player who rigidly insists that town cannot vote without an obvious mistake is creating an environment where mafia never face real heat.

That doesn't mean we spray votes recklessly, but it does mean pressure votes based on game-state management and evasive or over-cautious posture are entirely valid today. I share your skepticism of Felix's stance—it sounds structured and disciplined on the surface, but functionally it works to paralyze town decision-making.

Lucia, your Day 1 standard was explicit: you would vote only on a concrete contradiction, an unverifiable or conflicting night claim, or a clear refusal to answer fair questions. Today you endorse behavioral cases and “game-state management,” then call Felix’s caution functionally paralyzing. That is a different standard, not an application of yours. It also turns “over-cautious posture”—exactly the kind of behavioral read we largely ruled out Day 1—into a lynch reason. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
